type: u32 type index in object header word 0, indexing that file's own section-0 name table; the same class has a different index in every file, and the parsed name/index alignment drifts
structure: Type indices are per file and type names are not reliably aligned, so no cross-file tool may key on either

location.offset: the placement class is index 104 in Level_027_Tutorial, 95 in Challenge_Level_000, 97 in Challenge_Level_001, 98 in Level_000_Mining and 57 in the 001_Gryphon character archive; its model records are 64 / 53 / 55 / 58 / 9 in the same order

meaning: Two independent traps for any tool that reads more than one IGZ. First, the type INDEX is per file: hardcoding 104 for a placement reads igAlphaFunctionAttr or igGraphPathList in another level, which is why a first pass of the model resolver found 673 placements in the tutorial and zero everywhere else. Second, the type NAME is not a safe substitute: parseTypes splits section 0 on NUL and the name range is interrupted by 12-byte block records, so the index-to-name alignment drifts (1 358 of the tutorial's 2 858 header-table entries resolve to an empty name, and the placement class parses as igTransformSequence1_5 in the tutorial but as igAlphaFunctionAttr at the corresponding index elsewhere). The working rule is to DETECT a class structurally in each file, from the record layout, and to treat the parsed name as a label only. src/igz/model-resolve.mjs does this: it scores every class in the header table on a layout signature (world position at +0x24, heading at +0x34, scale 100 at +0xB8, a resolvable asset reference at +0xDC) and picks the dominant one, which is unambiguous in all five files tested (no runner-up scored above zero). Measured across the whole disc: 23 distinct indices hold placements depending on the file, which is why nothing may key on the number.
